newsitem.title: USA: NHL ICE HCOKEY-WINGS GOALIE VERNON BACK ON TOP OF HOCKEY WORLD.
newsitem.headline: NHL ICE HCOKEY-WINGS GOALIE VERNON BACK ON TOP OF HOCKEY WORLD.

text.p: Mike Vernon stood happily in the Detroit dressing room, still calm in the face of a raucus victory celebration after the Red Wings had defeated the Philadelphia Flyers Saturday to with the Stanley Cup in the minimum four games.
Vernon had been named the winner of the Conn Smythe Trophy as the playoffs most valuable player after posting a phenomenal 1.76 goals against average over 20 playoff games.
Not bad for the goat of the 1995 finals and a man who looked about to be traded earlier this season.
At 34, Vernon was considered washed up two years ago after he was bombed in the 1995 NHL finals by the New Jersey Devils in a sweep of the heavily-favoured Red Wings.
"I think we all had in the back of our minds two years ago how devastating it was to lose to Jersey," he said.

"I was just glad that I had the opportunity to prove myself again and I think we all had that in mind," said Vernon, who was in goal for all 16 Detroit post-season wins, suffering just four losses along the way.
Back in March, after serving as the backup to much younger Chris Osgood all season, Vernon was on the trading block.
But suddenly at playoff time, Detroit coach Scotty Bowman ignored all advice and made Vernon, who had only 13 regular season wins, his playoff goaltender.
"Mike had won the Stanley Cup in 1989 with the Calgary Flames," said Bowman, who knows a little something about winning Stanley Cups after collecting his seventh as a coach Saturday.
"When we traded for him three years ago we wanted that experience. Chris Osgood is a real fine young goalie and his time will come. But Vernon was the man in these playoffs."

The man indeed, in out-dueling former Stanley Cup winning goaltenders such as St Louis' Grant Fuhr in the first round and the great Patrick Roy in the semifinal victory over defending champions Colorado.
In the finals, the smallish Vernon stood tall in the net and was far superior to the outclassed Flyers tandem of Ron Hextall and Garth Snow.
On Saturday, one fan at Joe Louis Arena even held up a sign, apologising to Vernon for questioning his ability.
"I don't know who the guy was who did the apologising, but I accept it," said the good-natured veteran.
"Two summers ago they took an offer off the table and I thought I was out of work," he recalled.
Now, because of a special Cup-winning clause in his contract, Vernon now has the right to renew with Detroit for one more year at $2.3 million. But nothing is definite.
"As we have just seen you never know what is going to happen," Vernon said.
"I thought I was insurance for Scotty in case something happened to Osgood.
"Suddenly, we get to March and I thought they would trade me. They don't and I'm the goalie," he said in describing the strange turn of events that made him the hero of the hour.
"Chris handled it good. He could have blown some steam, but he acted as a professional and I think he knows he is the Wings goalie of the future."
What does that make Vernon?
"I'm just the old guy who won the Cup," he laughed.
